meta.title: Two Roads to the Same Mode
meta.summary: Relative tells you where a mode's notes are; parallel tells you what changed about its sound — and this pathway leads with the one that actually answers what you came for.

spans.text: Ask where a mode's notes live and you get one answer. Ask what changed about how it sounds and you get a completely different one — and mixing the two up is why "just think of the parent scale" leaves so many players able to name a mode's notes and unable to make it sound like anything. This pathway leads with the second question and treats the first as a shortcut worth knowing, not a destination.
Relative
keeps the notes and moves the home. A Dorian and G major share every letter —
A B C D E F# G

— so if you already know G major's shapes, you already know A Dorian's notes, full stop. On a guitar that's worth a fortune: no new fingers, no new fretboard geography, just a different note to call home. You met this move already, for minor, in
The Same Seven Notes
Parallel
keeps the home and moves the notes. A Dorian is A Aeolian with its
b6
raised to a natural
— same root, six shared notes, one moved. You met this move too, for minor, in
The Three Notes That Drop
The relative road needs one lookup, and here it is for all seven — the major scale each mode on
A
borrows its notes from:

A parent scale is worth naming only when you're using the relative road to find notes fast. It's never how you identify a mode by ear, and nothing in that table tells you what any of these seven sound like.
Both cards above hold exactly the same seven pitches — A Dorian's parent really is G major, note for note. Hold
G
underneath the first and it's G major. Hold
A
underneath the second and it's A Dorian. The note list never moved an inch; only what it was measured against did. That G card is the only scale in this chapter built on a root other than
A
, and it's here on purpose — a parent scale can't be demonstrated without playing it.

Now put the parent scale down. Use relative to find A Dorian's notes fast if you need to, then stop thinking in G. A player holding "this is G major" in their head while trying to sound like A Dorian is aiming at the wrong note, and the shapes will keep pulling the ear back toward G — exactly what
Same Notes, Different Home
warned about for C major and A minor. That's the real reason this pathway stays on one root: seven modes on
A
can be compared note against note, and that comparison is the lesson relative can't give you.
If you want the relative shortcut drilled further,
Same Hand, Different Key
is a fair detour — same move, just practised across more keys.
You can now find any mode's notes, and you know which road answers which question. So once actual chords are playing underneath — not just a held root — what keeps the ear at home at all?
